extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science, comparative government, and readers of Tocqueville
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Tocqueville’s evaluative principles and institutional standards for local and state administration in the United States (township, county, courts, legislature, governor). Focus is on how laws are enforced, checks on elected officers, and the political effects of local vs central administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for enforcing execution of the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Society has only two general methods of enforcing the execution of the laws: (1) entrusting a discretionary power to a superior functionary who can direct and cashier subordinates; or (2) authorizing the courts of justice to inflict judicial penalties on the offender.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville notes these two methods are not always both available (especially where many officers are elected). He uses this dichotomy to evaluate regimes’ ability to compel obedience and to justify judicial oversight when administrative hierarchical control is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inalienability of elective functions and its consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: An elected magistrate can neither be cashiered nor promoted; elective functions are inalienable until their term expires, so an elected magistrate has 'nothing either to expect or to fear from his constituents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because election severs the link between issuing orders and holding power to punish or reward, ‘the double right of commanding and of enforcing obedience can never be vested in the same individual,’ producing lack of gradation and complicating administrative control. Tocqueville treats this as a structural evaluative criterion when judging systems that rely heavily on election.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of judicial power to counterbalance elective authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: An elective authority which is not subject to judicial power will sooner or later either elude all control or be destroyed; the courts of justice are the only possible medium between central power and administrative bodies and alone can compel elected functionaries to obey without violating electors’ rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville argues that 'the extension of judicial power in the political world ought therefore to be in the exact ratio of the extension of elective offices.' Use this as a standard for institutional design: where many offices are elective, judicial remedies must be robust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and character of Justices of the Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: The Justice of the Peace is a mezzo termine between the magistrate and the man of the world, obligated to execute police regulations; good sense and integrity are often more valuable than legal science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville values justices for introducing 'established forms and publicity' that resist despotism, while not being blinded by legal superstition. He contrasts English/American usage and notes American adaptation (less aristocratic); evaluate their utility by how they combine administrative and judicial functions at local level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court of Sessions as mixed administrative and political tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: In Massachusetts the Court of Sessions (composed of justices) is both an administrative body and a political tribunal: it meets twice a year and is empowered to enforce the obedience of a majority of public officers; it presides over county affairs and acts judicially when town administration is brought before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville treats the Court of Sessions as an institutional model for where judicial procedure is used to inform and guarantee administration; when assessing local institutions, note whether they function purely administrative, purely judicial, or mixed as in Massachusetts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial formality as a means of concealing and enforcing executive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States the authority of the Government is often 'mysteriously concealed under the forms of a judicial sentence'; fines and judicial mandates (executed by sheriff) are used to enforce township obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is an evaluative lens: judicial processes are used instrumentally to enforce administrative obligations without openly appearing as executive coercion—assess whether this preserves liberties or masks executive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of public-officer misconduct and justiciability
rubrics_metrics.description: All reprehensible actions of public functionaries reduce to: (1) executing the law without energy or zeal; (2) neglecting to execute the law; (3) doing what the law enjoins him not to do. Only the last two (positive neglect or illegal action) can be brought under the cognizance of a tribunal because a 'positive and appreciable fact' is indispensable for an action at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This delineation is a practical criterion: legal systems can punish neglect or illegal acts but struggle to compel zeal or competence; institutional remedies must account for the unjudiciable nature of lukewarm obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of courts in compelling zeal or competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts cannot compel a public officer to greater ability, zeal, or energy when he obeys the letter of the law; the only effective check against quasi-offences (negligence or lukewarmness) is the possibility of arbitrary removal or electoral accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to evaluate administrative accountability: legal remedies are insufficient for performance; mechanisms of removal/election or supervisory inspection are necessary to secure active obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of remedies for public officer failings
rubrics_metrics.description: Tocqueville’s tripartite remedy system: (1) ordinary courts punish crimes committed in function; (2) administrative tribunals punish faults of official capacity; (3) annual popular tribunals (electors) remove those guilty of intangible offences of which 'human justice has no cognizance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing governance systems, check whether such differentiated remedies exist and whether they function in practice (timeliness, accessibility, effectiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulties of prosecuting administrative offences and division of prosecutorial roles
rubrics_metrics.description: There is often no public prosecutor in administrative tribunals; Americans divide inspection and prosecution: grand jurors, fiscal officers (treasurer), or private plaintiffs (incentivized by shares of fines) bring prosecutions. Reliance on private interest is frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tocqueville warns this creates gaps: if individual interest is insufficient, laws may fall into disuse. When evaluating enforcement structures, examine presence of dedicated prosecutors and reliance on private incentives (e.g., qui tam-like shares).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pecuniary incentives for informers
rubrics_metrics.description: American legislation often awards a portion of the penalty to the informer/plaintiff (e.g., half the fine) to encourage prosecution of administrative neglect where public interest alone may not motivate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit policy tool and a normative trade-off: it promotes enforcement but 'insures the execution of the laws by the dangerous expedient of degrading the morals of the people.' Evaluate effectiveness versus moral/externalities costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local institutional variation across States (township vs county)
rubrics_metrics.description: Activity and perfection of local authorities decrease toward the South; the township is the mainspring of administration in Massachusetts but as one moves south/west importance shifts from township to county, with county assemblies in NY/Ohio/Pennsylvania exercising taxation and executive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regional variation as a criterion: assess how institutional form (township vs county) affects citizen participation, administrative activity, and the balance between local and central powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of subsidiarity: individuals best judge their own concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Township and county rest on the principle that 'everyone is the best judge of what concerns himself alone, and the most proper person to supply his private wants.' The State governs broadly but does not interfere with local administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This normative principle is Tocqueville’s explanatory standard for decentralized institutions; evaluate arrangements by how well they reflect local knowledge and avoid unnecessary central interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of electing public officers and absence of gradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because officers are elected or chosen from among citizens and terms are limited, it is impossible to establish a dependent series of authorities; there are 'almost as many independent functionaries as there are functions,' disseminating executive power among many hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural trait is evaluative: it increases independence and local control but creates need for judicial controls and pecuniary penalties to enforce compliance. Use it to judge administrative coherence and accountability trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal characteristics of American administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Tocqueville summarizes: election of public officers (inalienability), absence of a gradation of ranks, and the introduction of judicial control over secondary branches are universal features of the American system from Maine to the Floridas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these three characteristics as a checklist when comparing U.S. states or other polities to Tocqueville’s model of American administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between central government and central administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization has two meanings: (1) central government — power over general national interests; (2) central administration — concentration of local administrative direction. They can coincide but are distinct and have different political effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analytical distinction when evaluating 'centralization' claims: a polity may have a strong central government yet decentralized local administration, with differing consequences for public spirit and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political effects of administrative centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: A central administration enervates nations by diminishing public spirit; while it can concentrate resources effectively in crises, it weakens renewal of national resources and long-term public vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a normative criterion: prefer centralized government for certain functions but be wary of centralized administration eroding civic engagement; weigh short-term efficiency vs long-run civic health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the legislative body into two houses: purpose and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative power is divided into two branches (Senate and House of Representatives) to divide legislative power, check assemblies, and provide a tribunal of appeal for revision of laws. The Senate usually has longer terms to preserve a nucleus of experienced legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an evaluative standard for bicameralism: assess whether the upper chamber provides stability and a moderating influence without creating aristocratic dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office and powers of the Governor in a State
rubrics_metrics.description: The Governor represents executive power but enjoys only part of it: he is moderator and counsellor of the legislature, has veto/suspensive power, lays wants before legislature, executes decrees, commands the militia, and must act in emergencies; yet he is dependent on the people due to short terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the executive in state constitutions, check for presence of veto power, emergency/executive responsibilities, military command, and term length as indicators of independence vs dependence on popular will.
